section.title: The Year of the Lord's Favor
section.sectionRationale: This is the passage Jesus stands and reads in the synagogue at Nazareth, then rolls up the scroll and says, today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing, Luke 4:16-21. He stops mid-sentence, before the day of our God's vengeance, a deliberate pause that shapes how the whole chapter, and the two advents of Christ, must be read.
section.thesis: The Spirit-anointed Servant brings good news to the poor, freedom to captives, and comfort to mourners, inaugurating the year of the LORD's favor now in His first coming, while the day of vengeance He named but did not yet enact awaits His return.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Spirit's anointing and the Servant's mission; rebuilding, double honor, and an everlasting covenant; and the Servant's own rejoicing, robed in salvation as a bridegroom and bride.

units.label: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me

verses.text: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has {{mashach|anointed}} Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners,
to proclaim the {{ratzon|year of the LORD’s favor}} and the day of our God’s vengeance, to comfort all who mourn,

to console the mourners in Zion, to give them a crown of beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and a garment of praise for a spirit of despair. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified.

units.label: Rebuild, restore, a double portion
units.note: priests of the LORD, an everlasting covenant

verses.text: They will rebuild the ancient ruins; they will restore the places long devastated; they will renew the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations.
Strangers will stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners will be your plowmen and vinedressers.
But you will be called the priests of the LORD; they will speak of you as ministers of our God; you will feed on the wealth of nations, and you will boast in their riches.

Instead of shame, My people will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation, they will rejoice in their share; and so they will inherit a double portion in their land, and everlasting joy will be theirs.
For I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity; in My faithfulness I will give them their recompense and make an everlasting covenant with them.
Their descendants will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples. All who see them will acknowledge that they are a people the LORD has blessed.

units.label: Clothed with garments of salvation
units.note: a bridegroom, a bride, righteousness springing up

verses.text: I will rejoice greatly in the LORD, my soul will exult in my God; for He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
For as the earth brings forth its growth, and as a garden enables seed to spring up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.

mashach.gloss: To anoint, to consecrate by pouring oil, the verb behind the noun Mashiach, Messiah, the Anointed One. The Speaker is anointed by the Spirit for a specific mission, good news, healing, liberty, exactly the mission Jesus claims for Himself when He reads this passage and says, today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing, Luke 4:21.

ratzon.gloss: The year of favor or acceptance, likely evoking the Year of Jubilee, Leviticus 25, when debts were forgiven, slaves freed, and land restored. Jesus stops His reading of this verse exactly at favor, before the day of vengeance, deliberately marking His first coming as the proclamation of favor, with the day of vengeance reserved for His return.

basic.context: This is the passage Jesus reads aloud in His hometown synagogue and then declares fulfilled in Himself, Luke 4:16-21. A Spirit-anointed figure announces good news to the poor, freedom for captives, and comfort for mourners, in language that recalls the Year of Jubilee, a season of release and restoration.
basic.hermeneutics: Jesus' own use of this text is the interpretive key: He reads up through comfort all who mourn and stops there, closing the scroll before the day of our God's vengeance. This deliberate pause teaches that His first coming inaugurates the favor while the vengeance awaits His second coming, a two-advent structure the church has always recognized.
basic.originalLanguages: The Speaker is mashach, anointed, by the Spirit, the very word behind Messiah. He proclaims the shenat ratzon, the year of favor, evoking the Jubilee's release of captives and restoration of land, a season of grace Jesus announces as beginning in Himself.
basic.typology: The anointed Herald preaching good news to the poor and binding up the brokenhearted anticipates and is fulfilled in Christ's earthly ministry. The double portion and everlasting covenant for a once-shamed people anticipate the church's inheritance in Christ. The garments of salvation and robe of righteousness anticipate the wedding imagery of Christ and His bride in Revelation 19.
basic.christ: Jesus reads this exact passage in Luke 4:16-21 and declares, today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing, applying the Spirit's anointing and the mission of good news, liberty, and comfort directly to Himself, while deliberately stopping before the day of vengeance, since His first coming brings grace, and His second coming will bring final judgment.
basic.god: God is both merciful and just, and this chapter holds the two together without confusion, He loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity, verse 8, even while proclaiming a year of favor to the brokenhearted and captive; His justice is not canceled by His mercy, it is simply not yet fully unveiled.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 4:16-21 has Jesus read this passage and apply it directly to Himself. Leviticus 25 describes the Year of Jubilee this passage evokes. Revelation 19:7-8 pictures the bride clothed for her wedding, echoing verse 10's bridegroom and bride imagery.
basic.oneStory: A Spirit-anointed figure was promised who would announce a year of favor, release captives, and comfort mourners, stopping short of final judgment until a later day. Jesus stands in a synagogue, reads these very words, and says they are fulfilled in Him, marking His first coming as the opening of grace and His return as the day this chapter also names but does not yet unleash.

context.literary:
Isaiah 61 begins with a voice that speaks in the first person, 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me', and the first three verses are one long sentence of purpose. A string of infinitives carries the mission: to preach good news, to bind up, to proclaim liberty, to proclaim the year of favor and the day of vengeance, to comfort, to console, to give. Then the poem turns outward. Verses 4 to 9 describe what the restored people will do and become, in the third person, rebuilding ruins, serving as priests and receiving a double portion. Verses 10 and 11 return to the first person with a song of rejoicing. The shape runs from the one who is sent, to the people who receive, to a voice of praise.

Verse 3 is a small masterpiece of exchange. Three times a bad thing is replaced by a good one with the little word 'for', which in Hebrew means 'in place of': a crown for ashes, oil of joy for mourning, a garment of praise for a spirit of despair. The pattern is repeated in verse 7, where shame is replaced by a double portion, and verse 1 to 3 closes with a statement of why: 'that He may be glorified.' Isaiah 60:21 ended in the same way, so that both chapters end their opening movement with God's glory as the goal.

The chapter is tied closely to what comes before and after. Chapter 60 describes the glory of the city, 61 introduces the person who brings it about, and 62 returns to the city with a new name and a bridegroom. Within the book, the speaker of verse 1 shares the language of the Servant: the Spirit upon him as in 42:1, a mouth and a mission as in 49:1-3 and 50:4. This is where a long thread of promises about a Spirit-anointed deliverer comes to a point.
context.historical:
The background to verses 1 and 2 is the law of Jubilee. In Leviticus 25 the horn was sounded on the Day of Atonement in the fiftieth year, liberty was proclaimed throughout the land, and each person returned to his property and clan, Leviticus 25:8-13. Debts were released, bound servants went free and land went back to its families. The key word is deror, liberty, which appears in Leviticus 25:10 and in Jeremiah 34:8, where King Zedekiah's covenant to proclaim liberty to slaves was made and then broken, and in Ezekiel 46:17 as 'the year of freedom'. By setting the mission in Jubilee terms, Isaiah says that the coming deliverance will be a release that works at the level of persons, families and land.

The first hearers were a community that knew what ruins looked like. Verse 4 speaks of 'ancient ruins' and 'the desolations of many generations', and the returned exiles lived among broken walls and abandoned fields. Ashes and mourning were the customary signs of grief, and sitting in ashes was an act of lament. A crown, oil and a festive garment were the signs of celebration, as at a wedding or an anointing. The people who heard this would have understood the exchanges of verse 3 as the end of a long funeral.

Anointing with oil was the way Israel set apart kings and priests, and sometimes prophets, as when Elisha is to be anointed 'as prophet', 1 Kings 19:16. To say that the speaker has been anointed by the LORD claims an office, but the anointing here is by the Spirit, which is a mark of the Servant in 42:1. The 'foreigners' of verse 5 who feed the flocks and tend the vineyards reflect the actual shape of agricultural labour in the ancient world, a role that leaves the Israelites free for the priestly service in verse 6. In the post-exilic setting, where Zechariah saw the high priest Joshua in filthy garments and then clothed in splendid robes, Zechariah 3:3-5, the garments of verse 10 would have had a strong ring.
context.canonical:
This is the passage Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth, and a careful look at Luke 4:18-19 shows how much he does with it. Luke's text follows the Greek of Isaiah in saying 'recovery of sight to the blind', which is how the Greek translated the Hebrew for opening, and it adds the phrase 'to release the oppressed' from Isaiah 58:6. Jesus then stops in the middle of verse 2 at 'the year of the Lord's favor', rolls up the scroll and says 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing', Luke 4:20-21. He leaves out 'the day of vengeance of our God', and he does not read 'bind up the brokenhearted' or 'comfort all who mourn' in the version Luke records. The omission of vengeance sets the two comings of the Messiah apart.

Elsewhere in the Gospels the same chapter lies behind Jesus' answer to John the Baptist in prison, 'the blind receive sight... and the good news is preached to the poor', Matthew 11:5, which joins Isaiah 61 with Isaiah 35:5-6. The Beatitudes for the poor and for those who mourn, Matthew 5:3-4, are drawn from the same ground. Acts 10:38 says that God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and Paul uses the idea of a year of favor in 2 Corinthians 6:2, quoting Isaiah 49:8 and declaring 'now is the time of favor'.

The other half of the pairing in verse 2 returns in Isaiah 34:8 and 63:4, where the day of vengeance is joined to the year of redemption, and in 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8, where Christ is revealed from heaven in judgment. The promise that God's people will be priests links verse 6 to Exodus 19:6, 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 1:6. The garments and bridal imagery of verse 10 lead to Revelation 19:7-8, where the bride is given fine linen, and to Revelation 21:2, where the city is adorned as a bride for her husband.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted a people who had been in mourning to hear the language of a feast. After exile, ruin and slow disappointment, the book now says that someone has been sent, by the Spirit and with a clear commission, to turn their sorrow into joy. The details are carefully chosen. The poor, the brokenhearted, the captives and the mourners are the people who have no power to rescue themselves. The message is that deliverance is aimed at those who need it, and the gospel is first good news to them.

He also wanted them to see that the deliverance would come as a gift and would then set them to work. Verse 3 ends with God being glorified, but verses 4 to 6 describe the people rebuilding ruins and serving as priests. The restored are not spectators. They become the ones who repair what generations had left in ruins, and they are called to a priestly role among the nations. This is a pattern of grace producing mission.

A third aim lies in verse 8, where God says He loves justice and hates robbery. The previous chapters had shown a community that tolerated injustice, Isaiah 59:14. The prophet wants it understood that restoration is not a way around justice but a way of establishing it, and that the everlasting covenant of verse 8 rests on the character of God, 'in My faithfulness.' Finally, the rejoicing of verses 10 and 11 is meant to be shared. The hearers are invited to join in the song of clothing and planting, and to see that righteousness and praise are what God makes spring up before all the nations.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is mostly promise and description of what the Spirit-anointed one will do. It is not a command to anyone to take up that mission in his own name. The first person who speaks is the bearer of a particular office, and the church has never understood these verses as a job description for any person who feels moved. At the same time, the effects of His work are described as passed on: the oaks of righteousness are called to rebuild, and the priests of the LORD are called to serve. Believers share in the mission as those who have received its benefits, which is why Jesus sends His disciples in the same Spirit, John 20:21.

Care is needed in the second half. The foreigners who work the fields and the wealth of nations that the people eat describe the world of the first hearers, and they are not a charter for domination of others. Verse 8 is about God's own love of justice, and it does not give permission to exact retribution. Jesus' stopping before the day of vengeance is the model for how to apply the passage today. The church is to hold out the year of favor with open hands and to leave the day of vengeance to God, in line with Romans 12:19, while still believing that He will in the end set all wrongs right.

debates.question: Who is the speaker in verses 1 to 3?

views.label: The Servant of the LORD, and so the Messiah
views.case: The Spirit resting on the speaker echoes Isaiah 42:1 and 11:2, and the sending and the mouth recall 49:1-3 and 50:4. The Servant's work of opening blind eyes and bringing prisoners out of the dungeon, Isaiah 42:7, matches the freedom of verse 1. Jesus identifies Himself as the speaker in Luke 4:21, and Acts 10:38 reads His life in these terms. This is the dominant Christian reading.

views.label: The prophet himself, or the prophetic community
views.case: The anointing of a prophet is attested in the Old Testament, as with Elisha in 1 Kings 19:16, and Isaiah 48:16 has a speaker who says 'the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit.' On this view the speaker is a prophet announcing good news to the returned exiles, and the passage later became a pattern for the Messiah. Many scholars hold this as the original voice.

views.label: A prophetic voice that comes to rest in the Messiah
views.case: The two readings are often joined. The prophet speaks with the voice of the Servant, so that the passage describes a prophetic mission that finds its full form in the Anointed One. This allows the original setting and the New Testament fulfilment to stand together.

debates.bearing: Whatever the original speaker, Jesus' use of the text is the key. Anointed with the Spirit, He brings the content of the passage into effect in His own ministry, Luke 4:21 and Matthew 11:5. The question of the original voice does not change what the New Testament says He accomplished.

debates.question: What does Jesus' stopping before the day of vengeance mean?

views.label: Two comings of the Messiah
views.case: The Lord reads the line about the year of favor and leaves the line about the day of vengeance, so that the first coming brings grace and the second brings judgment. Texts such as 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8 describe a revealing from heaven in judgment. This reading is common and fits the whole pattern of the New Testament.

views.label: Vengeance is itself redemptive, accomplished at the cross
views.case: Isaiah 63:4 puts the day of vengeance and the year of redemption together in one scene. Some read the cross as the place where judgment on sin and rescue of sinners happen at once, Romans 3:25-26, so that vengeance is not simply postponed. The omission is then about emphasis, not about separation.

views.label: The line is part of the same message but is not Jesus' present focus
views.case: Others note that the full promise remains one promise, and that Jesus stops because the fulfilment that day was about favor, with judgment still to follow. They stress that the two halves of the verse are the one work of God seen from two sides.

debates.bearing: All views agree that the favor is available now, and that judgment is real and certain. The second reading helps to guard against supposing that vengeance is simply left out. The text of Luke 4 recorded no more than the favor, and the rest of the New Testament adds that the day will come.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb 'anointed' in verse 1 is mashach, the source of the word Messiah, and the claim of verse 1 is that the LORD has anointed the speaker with the Spirit. Anointing by oil set apart kings, priests and sometimes prophets, as Elisha at 1 Kings 19:16. Here the oil is the Spirit, which is why Acts 10:38 says that God 'anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power'. The Greek form of the root gives us Christos, so that when Luke 4:18 has 'He has anointed Me', the name Christ is in the background.

The word for the 'brokenhearted' means those whose heart is broken, and the verb 'bind up' is the verb used for bandaging a wound. Ezekiel 34:4 uses the same verb of the shepherds who failed to bind up the injured. The speaker is therefore a shepherd who does what the faithless shepherds did not do. The care is physical in its picture and tender in its meaning.

In verse 1 the 'liberty' to be proclaimed is deror, a technical term for the release of the Jubilee, Leviticus 25:10, and for the freeing of slaves in Jeremiah 34:8. The verb 'proclaim' is the ordinary word for calling out, and it is the verb used in Leviticus 25:10 for proclaiming liberty. The phrase for the prisoners' freedom is a doubled Hebrew expression, a form of opening, which can refer to the opening of prison doors or of eyes. The Septuagint takes it as 'recovery of sight to the blind', and that is the form Luke quotes. The BSB footnote marks that wording as the Greek reading. Jesus' ministry of opening blind eyes therefore fits a reading already present in the Greek Bible.

Verse 2 has 'the year of the LORD's favor', where favor is ratzon, acceptance or pleasure. The word has come up in Isaiah 60:7 for sacrifices going up 'with acceptance' and in 60:10 for the favor in which God shows mercy. The Hebrew year is shanah, and the phrase marks a season in which God's pleasure rests on His people. Isaiah 49:8 has the same note in 'the time of favor', which Paul reads as now in 2 Corinthians 6:2. Set against it, 'the day of vengeance' is naqam. The vengeance is God's, and Isaiah 34:8 and 63:4 use the same pairing, so that the verse draws on a recognizable contrast of favor and judgment.

In verse 3 the Hebrew relies on sound. 'Crown of beauty for ashes' is pe'er tachat efer, with two words that echo each other. The pe'er is a headdress or turban, a mark of festivity or priestly dress. The same word returns in verse 10, where the bridegroom 'wears a priestly headdress', using a verb related to kohen, priest. Verse 3 and verse 10 therefore frame the passage with the same ornament, first given by God and then worn by the rejoicing speaker. The word for 'for' in 'for ashes', tachat, is repeated in each of the three exchanges and in verse 7, and carries the sense of 'in the place of'.

The people are called 'oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD', and the word for righteousness, tsedaqah, is the one in verse 10, 'robe of righteousness', and verse 11, 'righteousness and praise'. Verse 11 says God will cause them to 'spring up', which uses the verb behind the word for the Branch in Jeremiah 33:15, 'I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch'. The garden of verse 11 brings the images of growth and righteousness together, with the Branch hope of the prophets close by.

Finally, in verse 6 the people are 'priests of the LORD' and 'ministers of our God', and the language recalls the covenant at Sinai, 'a kingdom of priests', Exodus 19:6.

typology.type: The anointed herald of good news and release, verses 1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: The Spirit-anointed one proclaims liberty, in the pattern of Jubilee. In Luke 4:16-21 Jesus announces the passage fulfilled, and His ministry delivers its pieces: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, release from demons and sickness, Matthew 11:5 and Acts 10:38. The Jubilee was a year in the calendar, a single season of release every fifty years. Jesus brings a release that reaches deeper, freedom from sin itself, as He says in John 8:36, 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.' The pattern falls short because the Jubilee could return land and free servants but could not set a conscience free.

typology.type: The year of the LORD's favor, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: A season in which God's pleasure rests on His people. Paul writes that 'now is the time of favor, now is the day of salvation,' 2 Corinthians 6:2, taking a related promise from Isaiah 49:8 and placing it in the present. The Jubilee year pointed to a longer era of grace, and Christ opens that era at His first coming. Because Jesus stopped reading before the day of vengeance, the type has an open end: the age of favor continues until His return in judgment, 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8. The year of Jubilee fell short because it came once in fifty years, whereas the favor in Christ is open to all who come.

typology.type: Beauty for ashes, oil of joy, garment of praise, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The exchange of mourning for celebration prefigures the reversal brought by Christ. Zechariah 3:3-5 pictures a high priest in filthy clothes given splendid robes, and the Gospel parallels appear in the welcome of the returning son in the parable, Luke 15:22. Paul tells believers they have been clothed with Christ, Galatians 3:27. Hebrews 1:9 speaks of Christ Himself anointed with the oil of joy above His companions. The pattern is real and imperfect. Ashes and oil were outward signs that could be put on and taken off, while the gift of Christ's righteousness is a standing that cannot be lost.

typology.type: The people as priests who rebuild, verses 4 to 6
typology.fulfillment: The restored people repair ruins and are called priests of the LORD. At Sinai Israel was told it would be a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:6, and Peter applies that to the church, 'a royal priesthood, a holy nation', 1 Peter 2:9, and Revelation 1:6 says Christ has made us a kingdom, priests to His God. The church rebuilds ruined lives and communities in His name and brings the worship of the nations to God, Romans 15:16. The picture falls short in that the first priests served at a physical altar for a single nation, whereas the new priesthood draws from every nation and offers spiritual sacrifices through Christ, 1 Peter 2:5.

typology.type: The bridegroom and the bride, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: The speaker is clothed like a bridegroom and a bride, a picture of joy and splendour. The New Testament takes up marriage as the picture of Christ and His people. John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom, John 3:29, Paul speaks of Christ presenting the church to Himself 'glorious, without stain or wrinkle', Ephesians 5:25-27, and Revelation 19:7-8 shows the bride given fine linen. The garments of salvation are given and not earned. The type falls short because earthly marriage is temporary, whereas the union of Christ with His church is permanent.

study.christ:
Of all the chapters in this part of Isaiah, this is the one where Jesus most openly says that it is about Him. In Nazareth He finds the place, reads, rolls up the scroll, sits down, and says, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing,' Luke 4:21. The chapter leads to Christ first as the person described in verses 1 to 3. The Spirit of the Lord was on Him at the Jordan, Luke 3:22, and He came into Galilee 'in the power of the Spirit', Luke 4:14. To be anointed is to be the Christ, and the first sermon of His public ministry is a statement of what it means for Him to be the Anointed One.

Each element of the commission is then seen at work. Good news to the poor is preached in the Beatitudes, Matthew 5:3, and listed among His signs when John's disciples ask if He is the One, Matthew 11:2-5. Sight is given to the blind, captives are freed from demons and disease, and mourners are comforted, as when the widow of Nain's son is raised, Luke 7:11-15. Jubilee is also in view. Debts are forgiven, and sins are forgiven with them, Luke 5:20, 7:47-48. The scroll is read as an agenda, and the Gospels are the account of how it was carried out.

The stopping point is a part of the lesson. Jesus reads to 'the year of the Lord's favor' and leaves out the day of vengeance. The Messiah of Isaiah 61 has two works and two times. At His first coming He announces and gives favor; at His second He will carry out the day of vengeance, and Paul says that He will be revealed from heaven in blazing fire, 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8. Until then, 'now is the time of favor', 2 Corinthians 6:2. The invitation is open and it will not remain open forever.

The chapter also leads to Christ as the source of the garments of verse 10. 'He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness' is the speech of someone who has been given a righteousness that is not his own. Christians are said to have clothed themselves with Christ, Galatians 3:27, and Paul's phrase 'the righteousness of God' is the same gift, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The final image of the garden in verse 11, where righteousness and praise spring up before all the nations, recalls the Branch who sprouts for David in Jeremiah 33:15.

Some restraint helps. The passage has its own first setting, and the church is not entitled to say that every phrase of verses 4 to 9 is secretly about Jesus. The rebuilding of ruins, the foreigners with the flocks and the double portion are about the restored people. What the New Testament claims for Christ is the commissioning in verses 1 to 3, the favor of verse 2 and the righteousness of verse 10. The rest is the harvest of that work in His people.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is Trinitarian in outline without saying so. 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me.' There is the Lord GOD who sends, the Spirit who rests on the speaker, and the one who is sent and anointed. Isaiah 48:16 and 63:10 have similar patterns. The later church read these texts as signs of the Father sending the Son in the power of the Spirit, which is exactly what Luke 4:14-21 shows.

God is also the God of the broken. The commission begins with the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives and the mourners, those who are weakest in the ancient world. He does not wait for them to become strong. He sends someone to bind up and to console. This is a doctrine of divine care: the Holy One of Israel stoops to people whose hearts are in pieces and treats their sorrow as a work to be done.

He is a God of reversals. A crown for ashes, oil for mourning, a garment for despair, a double portion for shame. The repeated word 'in place of' shows that He does not simply remove what is bad but replaces it with something better. Where Isaiah 40:2 said that Jerusalem had received double for her sins, here the double comes as a portion of blessing, a sign that the measure of grace is not the measure of the offence.

God is just. 'For I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity,' verse 8. The favor in verse 2 sits beside the vengeance, and both belong to the one God. Because He loves justice, He cannot ignore wrong, and so the year of favor is not a way of avoiding justice but a time of grace before it is fully executed. Mercy is not a lowering of standards. The everlasting covenant He makes rests on His faithfulness, so that the people are secure not in their own performance but in His word.

He is a God who glorifies Himself by making His people glad. The people are 'oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified.' The sequence is that He plants, they flourish, and He is praised. Verse 11 closes with the picture of a garden in which His own righteousness and praise grow in the sight of the nations. For worship, this means that our rejoicing is not a competitor to His glory. The right response to the chapter is the song of verse 10, 'I will rejoice greatly in the LORD', which is both gratitude for what has been given and the way He is praised.

crossReferences.note: The law of Jubilee: the horn sounds on the Day of Atonement, liberty is proclaimed to all the inhabitants, and each person returns to his property and clan. Isaiah 61:1-2 takes this institution and makes it the pattern of the coming deliverance. The shared word is liberty, and the shared idea is release that restores.

The Servant has the Spirit placed upon Him and is to open blind eyes and bring prisoners out of the dungeon. Those lines are the nearest parallel to Isaiah 61:1, and they show why the chapter has been read as the speech of the Servant, who is also a light to the nations, so that the mission is the same.

The fast God chooses is to break the chains of wickedness and set the oppressed free. Luke 4:18 combines this line with Isaiah 61:1, so that Jesus' reading joins release from chapter 58 to the anointing of chapter 61. Care for the oppressed is what the Anointed One brings and what His people are called to share.

Jesus reads from this scroll in the synagogue and says it is fulfilled that day. He stops at the year of the Lord's favor and leaves out the day of vengeance, and the whole scene is the interpretive key to the chapter. Everything the Gospel then records can be read as the working out of this announcement.

John the Baptist in prison asks whether Jesus is the One who was to come, and Jesus answers by pointing to the blind who see and the good news preached to the poor. The answer draws on Isaiah 61:1 and 35:5-6 together, and shows that He understood His works as the signs of the promised age.

A warrior comes with stained garments and says that the day of vengeance was in His heart and the year of His redemption had come. The two halves of Isaiah 61:2 are here joined in a single picture, which shows that vengeance and redemption are different sides of the same arrival, and helps explain why Jesus separated them in Luke 4.

Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8 and declares 'now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation.' His use of the phrase 'time of favor' shows the church reading the Isaianic language of favor as present, and it sets the urgency of the gospel invitation. The year of the LORD's favor has begun.

Believers are called a royal priesthood and a holy nation, to proclaim the excellencies of the One who called them out of darkness into His marvelous light. This takes up the priestly identity of Isaiah 61:6, which itself recalls Exodus 19:6, and gives the church the task of declaring praises that the chapter promised.

The high priest Joshua stands in filthy garments, and God removes his iniquity and clothes him in splendid robes with a clean turban. This is a close parallel to Isaiah 61:10 and its priestly headdress, and shows that the exchange of garments is a picture of forgiveness and restoration to service.

God promises to cause a righteous Branch to sprout for David, who will administer justice and righteousness. Isaiah 61:11 uses the same picture of causing righteousness to spring up, and the two together show that the growth of righteousness in the earth is bound to the coming of the Branch.

The marriage of the Lamb has come and the bride is given fine linen, bright and pure. This is the New Testament's version of Isaiah 61:10, where the one who rejoices is clothed like a bridegroom and a bride, and it shows that the garments of salvation reach their completion at the wedding of the Lamb.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a good world, and it is a world in which people are naked and unashamed. When sin enters, the mark of the fall is shame, and God's first act is to make clothing, Genesis 3:21. From there, the story is full of the signs of loss: ashes, mourning, captivity, ruins and a spirit of despair. Isaiah 61 gathers them one by one, and for each it names the replacement. It reads like the whole of Scripture's answer to the fall in a single chapter, with its exchange of garments, its release and its garden.

It also takes up a long line of institutions. Jubilee was Israel's periodic rehearsal of the idea that land and people belong to God and that debt and bondage do not have the last word. Prophets were anointed to speak for Him, and kings to rule for Him. Isaiah 61 draws these together in a figure who combines the anointing of prophet, king and priest, and who carries out the release that Jubilee only pictured. When the Jubilee was neglected, as in Jeremiah 34, the failure showed how much Israel needed a deliverer who would do what the law could not.

The chapter sits at the centre of the three chapters on the restored Zion. Chapter 60 shows the glory, 61 shows the one who brings it, and 62 gives the city a new name. In the Gospels, Jesus reads the central part of this and applies it to Himself. His first coming opens the year of favor, and His church now carries that message, as a people priested and sent. The unfinished half of verse 2 gives the Bible's story its tension between two comings.

At the end of the story, the exchange is completed. The wedding of the Lamb takes place and the bride is clothed in fine linen, Revelation 19:7-8. The former things pass away, and God wipes every tear from their eyes, with no more mourning, crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The ruins of many generations are replaced by a city, and the garden of Isaiah 61:11 gives way to a river and a tree of life, Revelation 22:1-2. Those who once sat in ashes will wear a crown, and the day of vengeance, no longer pending, will have done its work. Isaiah 61 is a promise that begins in a small synagogue and ends at a wedding, and in between, the Spirit-anointed Christ carries every part of it through.

sermon.title: Hope and Renewal: The Prophetic Vision of Zion's Restoration in Isaiah
sermon.why: Carson reads and expounds Isaiah 61:1 to 63:14 in this address, giving sustained attention to how Isaiah 61:1-2 is quoted by Jesus in Luke 4 and echoed in Matthew 11, tracing the passage's fulfillment in Christ's proclaimed mission of good news to the poor.

quiz.q: What happens when Jesus reads this passage in Luke 4:16-21?

options.text: He reads through comfort all who mourn, stops before the day of vengeance, and declares the Scripture fulfilled in Himself.
options.note: Luke 4:20-21 records Jesus' deliberate stopping point and His declaration of fulfillment.

options.text: He reads the entire passage including the day of vengeance and declares it all fulfilled that day.
options.note: He actually stops deliberately before the day of vengeance, a detail with real theological significance for how His first coming differs from His second.

options.text: He reads it but says it refers only to a future era, not to Himself.
options.note: He explicitly says, today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.

options.text: The Gospels never record Jesus reading from Isaiah in a synagogue.

quiz.q: What background does 'the year of the LORD's favor' most likely evoke?

options.text: The Year of Jubilee, when debts were forgiven, slaves freed, and land restored, Leviticus 25.
options.note: The language of liberty, release, and restoration closely matches Jubilee provisions.

options.text: An annual harvest festival with no connection to release or freedom.
options.note: The passage's emphasis on freedom for captives and prisoners points to Jubilee, not merely harvest themes.
The imagery is about release and restoration, not military triumph.
The weekly Sabbath shares the rhythm of rest, but the larger, cyclical release of the Jubilee year is the clearer background for this specific language.

quiz.q: Why is it significant that Jesus stops reading before 'the day of our God's vengeance'?

options.text: It shows His first coming proclaims grace and favor, while the day of vengeance awaits His second coming.
options.note: This reflects the New Testament's two-advent pattern, grace now, judgment at Christ's return.

options.text: It shows Jesus rejected the idea of any future judgment.
options.note: Other New Testament texts affirm a future day of judgment tied to Christ's return.

options.text: It shows the day of vengeance had already occurred before His ministry.
options.note: This misreads the timing; the vengeance is still future in New Testament teaching, tied to Christ's return, not something already past.

options.text: It has no theological significance and is simply where the reading happened to end.
options.note: The stopping point is widely understood as deliberate and theologically meaningful.

quiz.q: What image describes the Servant's own joy in verse 10?

options.text: Being clothed with garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness, like a bridegroom and bride adorned for a wedding.
options.note: Verse 10 uses explicit bridal and priestly imagery for the Servant's joy.

options.text: Being stripped of all honor and left in mourning clothes.
options.note: The opposite; the imagery is of celebratory adornment, not mourning.

options.text: Receiving a military crown after conquest.
options.note: It rightly senses triumph, but the imagery given is bridal and priestly, not militaristic.

options.text: Sitting silently with no outward expression of joy.
options.note: The verse explicitly says, I will rejoice greatly, and my soul will exult.

questions: Jesus claimed this passage as His own mission statement, good news to the poor, freedom to captives, comfort to mourners. Where in your life do you need to receive that good news rather than just admire it as someone else's story?

Jesus stopped reading before the day of vengeance, living now in the year of favor. How does knowing you live in the age of grace, not yet final judgment, shape how you treat people who are still far from God?
Verse 3 promises a crown of beauty for ashes, oil of joy for mourning. What ashes are you currently sitting in that you have not yet brought to God for that exchange?
The passage promises double honor to a once-shamed people. Where do you still carry old shame that God's covenant faithfulness says should already be behind you?
The Servant rejoices, clothed in garments of salvation like a bridegroom and bride. Does your own relationship with God feel like duty, or does it carry this same note of genuine celebration?

translationNotes.note: Luke 4:18 quotes this verse from the Greek Septuagint, which adds and recovery of sight to the blind, a phrase not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text but consistent with the passage's themes of release and restoration.

Jesus' reading in Luke 4:19 stops at to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor, omitting and the day of our God's vengeance to comfort all who mourn, a deliberate, well-recognized break in the citation.
